rv.q: Every once in a rare while, the theater rewards us with a kind of transcendent experience.
But in terms of conveying this work’s view of art as both a coolly isolating and warmly embracing experience, I’ve never seen a more convincing interpretation.

I felt unconstrained by the show's built-in artifice and was swept up by the vitality and simplicity of this production
You will be suitably swept away by Gyllenhaal's passionately acted, exquisitely articulated George.
But even as retooled, the show retains the quality of serene simplicity that heightens the poignant beauty of the score.
Gyllenhaal may be the main draw for ticket buyers, but this heavenly production is stronger than any one star.
The result is Sondheim’s most personal statement and thus, with all its odd corners and occasional wanderings, his most moving.

In this production, The Chromolume is a colorful moment of art that does not carry an obligation — and thus it is free to do what humans, riven by our need to both win the race and be loved along the way, can never do alone.

For the newest Broadway revival, though, we get not just humanity and warmth, but intimacy, tenderness, bursts of humor, and flashes of tremendous beauty -- we get, in effect, as accomplished a production of "Sunday in the Park with George" as we are likely to ever see.
This is a spectacular revival and the principals are simply breathtakingly good.
Like glass held up to the light, it’s shot through with intelligence and nuance and is all the more powerful for it.
They are, much like the production itself, mesmerizing and beautiful to watch.
But this stripped down Sunday doesn’t lack for its own theatrical delight and instead lets the characters’ yearnings fill the frame.
Its power to stir the heart and head with its radiant score and unfading story about the art of making art — and love — is as strong as ever.

In this format, Sunday in the Park With George warms the soul through its reminder that persistence and vision can overcome even the most daunting obstacles and help us see the world, however familiar it may be, in the blazing light of others' greatest imaginations.
It may feel a touch restrained in comparison with showier productions, but it boasts a skilful ensemble of stage vets.
The genius of Sunday in the Park With George is that it makes the audience feel those possibilities, too, and suggests they are just as important and compelling as the idea of love or marriage.
Given Gyllenhaal's film stardom, who knew, amid all that screen talent, he had such gorgeous pipes?
What a paradox that a musical so full of humanity and light could be built on the relentless exactitude of his inner questing.

Inarguably one of the greatest musicals of all time, it doesn’t take very long into Sarna Lapine’s revival to realize why this show needed to be back on Broadway: it’s become an allegory about the existence of musical theatre itself in an era of moral decay and ugliness prevailing over beauty.
Ms. Ashford is, as they are wont to say, simply divine.
Jake Gyllenhaal conquers the impossibilities of a Sondheim score with verve and ease.

"The actor’s performance, as the kids say (please forgive the pun), is quite on point...Gyllenhaal’s performance unveils seemingly endless surprises...In the hands of a less skilled actress, Dot and her scant backstory could easily become a trope of a discontented lover, but Ashford’s warmth and generosity mold this into an asset for her character..
The musical strikes a resonating chord—both in terms of its exploration of the creative process of making art, as well as the personal relationships that can crumble in its wake.
In the age of jukebox musicals, a show that overreaches is extremely welcome, especially since it's filled with such glistening insight, humor, and music.

Still, fans of this landmark musical will want to collect the performances of Gyllenhaal and Ashford; they'll also relish the opportunity to hear the score sung by a first-rate company, aided by Michael Starobin's gorgeous orchestrations.
